title: India Signs Rs 1,577 Crore Loiter-Munition Deals With Tata and NIBE as Army's Drone Drive Accelerates
subhead: New Delhi locked in contracts for long-range loitering munitions on the eve of a broader Rs 16,000 crore Army drone push, while a ProPublica investigation laid out the full scale of General Dynamics' failed $533 million artillery plant near Dallas.

sections.heading: India Signs Rs 1,577 Crore Loiter-Munition Contracts With Tata and NIBE
sections.body:
India's Ministry of Defence signed contracts worth approximately Rs 1,577 crore (roughly $1.6 billion) with Tata Advanced Systems Ltd (TASL) and NIBE Pvt Ltd for long-range loiter munition systems, according to multiple Indian defense news reports from Friday. The acquisition is aimed at enhancing the combat capability of the Army's artillery regiments. TASL and NIBE had emerged as the lowest bidders in the Army's tender to procure 840 loitering munitions with a range of around 100 km for a contract valued near Rs 1,600 crore.

The deal is the leading edge of a broader push: the Indian Army plans to procure drones worth around Rs 16,000 crore over the next two years, spanning surveillance and attack platforms. Prime Minister Narendra Modi, in his Independence Day speech on Saturday, stressed that India must develop indigenous drone and counter-drone capabilities, framing the procurement in self-reliance terms.
sections.whyItMatters: New Delhi is converting wartime drone lessons into domestic industrial programs, handing loiter-munition work to Indian firms rather than foreign primes — a concrete step in the country's longer-term goal of cutting import dependence in the unmanned sector.

sections.heading: ProPublica Lays Out General Dynamics' $533M Artillery Plant Failure
sections.body:
A ProPublica investigation (carried by Defense One on Aug. 15) details how a General Dynamics artillery factory near Dallas, funded by the U.S. Army for $533 million, has never produced a single usable shell. The plant was meant to churn out urgently needed 155mm artillery rounds for Ukraine, but its automated robots imported from Turkey repeatedly caught fire or malfunctioned — dropping steel, swinging out of control and cracking shells beyond repair. The U.S. Army ordered work halted on two of the factory's three production lines in August 2025 after General Dynamics missed eight deadlines.

A Department of Defense inspector general report in July confirmed the facility produced no usable rounds but offered few specifics and did not name the companies involved. The Army told ProPublica it plans to recover funding through discounts on future production orders with General Dynamics, which continues to oversee the site and declined to comment. The Army has not held General Dynamics or the Turkish subcontractor that supplied the equipment publicly accountable or demanded repayment.
sections.whyItMatters: The episode is a case study in how the surge to rebuild U.S. munitions production has stumbled: taxpayer money was spent, deadlines were blown and no output was delivered, yet the prime contractor kept winning new business — a gap between the rhetoric of artillery expansion and on-the-ground industrial reality.

sections.heading: Army Picks M1 Over Bell and Lockheed for $10B Helicopter Training Contract
sections.body:
The U.S. Army awarded M1 Support Services its Flight School Next contract — a firm-fixed-price, IDIQ worth up to $10 billion over 26 years — to convert the service's Initial Entry Rotary Wing school at Fort Rucker, Alabama, to a contractor-owned and -operated model, Defense One reported. The Texas-based company beat out Bell and Lockheed Martin (which had been dropped earlier in the competition). M1's team includes Robinson Helicopter Company, Quantum Helicopters, General Dynamics Information Technology and the University of North Dakota Aerospace Foundation; new pilots will train on the single-turbine Robinson R66, replacing the costlier twin-engine Airbus UH-72 Lakota.

Congress had blocked funding for the program in the National Defense Authorization Act pending a trial program, and it is not clear when the Army met those requirements before awarding the contract.
sections.whyItMatters: The award pushes Army pilot training toward an outsourcing model that trades government-owned aircraft and instructors for a commercial, contractor-run pipeline — a significant shift in how the service shapes its aviation force, and a notable competitive loss for two of the sector's biggest names.

sections.heading: Patriot Makers Hedge on Ukraine Production License as Kyiv's Industry Rises
sections.body:
Lockheed Martin and Raytheon have begun putting the brakes on a joint-production deal to build Patriot interceptors in Ukraine, Defense News reports, even after President Trump pledged Kyiv a license at the July NATO summit in Ankara. Executives are weighing what is 'feasible' as the licensing runs into Washington red tape, and Trump himself told the Financial Times on July 20 that the U.S. 'has to be a little bit careful of who we license to.' A Republican official on Capitol Hill told The Atlantic the real worry is that Ukraine could improve the Patriot and produce it at scale faster and cheaper, cutting into the U.S. monopoly on antiballistic capability — with companies framing concerns as 'IP theft and tech transfer' instead.

The context: the US-Iran war has drained an estimated two-thirds of America's pre-war Patriot interceptor inventory. Ukraine, nine European countries and firms including Eurosam, Leonardo, Thales and Saab have launched a coalition around Freyja, a new antiballistic system priced at roughly one-fifth of a Patriot round, and Lockheed unveiled its cheaper PAC-3 ACE round (about $2 million apiece) at Farnborough in July.
sections.whyItMatters: Zelenskyy said the two sides have 'now reached an agreement,' but the hedge shows how the world's biggest missile makers are reacting to a customer that has become a potential competitor — a structural shift in the antiballistic market driven by Ukraine's wartime production experience.

sections.heading: Pentagon Directs Up to $243.9M in No-Bid Spending on Palantir
sections.body:
Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg signed a memo directing Pentagon departments to commit up to $243.9 million to use Palantir's software through March 31, 2027, and to identify options for more spending through 2028, according to a memo viewed by Washington Technology. Feinberg said the software provides 'valuable support' to improve efficiencies with the defense industrial base, flagging delays in munitions and delivery-vehicle production. The memo cites none of the standard Federal Acquisition Regulation justifications for a no-compete contract.

No-compete contracts accounted for 14.8% of all federal awards in the first half of 2026, up from 12.6% a year earlier, and Palantir has received $3.2 billion in contract obligations since 2024, roughly half through no-compete awards. The company reported Q2 revenues of $1.9 billion, up 93% year over year, with federal contracts up 90%.
sections.whyItMatters: The directive is another data point in the growth of sole-source spending in U.S. defense IT, where a handful of software firms increasingly hold dominant positions without competitive pressure — a trend that has drawn scrutiny even as AI and data tools become central to Pentagon operations.

sections.heading: White House Revives 'Privateering for the Digital Age' With Authorized Offensive Cyber
sections.body:
The White House announced a policy (Aug. 12) under which the U.S. government will pay private cybersecurity companies to 'manipulate,' 'degrade,' 'disrupt' and 'destroy' foreign adversary computer networks. Companies will be vetted and supervised by the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security and forbidden from actions that could result in 'loss of life or serious injury,' per the presidential memo. Jeff Gray, a former DHS/CISA incident-response trainer, described it as 'reviving privateering for the digital age.'

Defense One's reporting notes Russia has long enlisted private groups for such operations, and that AI-assisted cyberattacks rose 89% in 2025 per a CrowdStrike threat report. One U.S. cybersecurity firm founder said the policy makes sense as adversaries gain AI tools.
sections.whyItMatters: The policy formalizes a growing reliance on private companies for offensive cyber operations — a private-military-and-security development in the digital domain that expands who can lawfully strike foreign networks and raises new accountability questions.

sections.heading: Russia's Sahel Air Bridge Persists, C4ADS Finds
sections.body:
A new analysis by the Center for Advanced Defense Studies (C4ADS), published Wednesday, found Russian state-aligned forces operating in the Central Sahel relied on at least 75 flights by military and military-linked aircraft between January 2025 and July 2026, based on ADS-B data from FlightRadar24. Burkina Faso received the most flights (56), followed by Mali (38) and Niger (6). The busiest operator was Flight Unit 224, a Russian Defense Ministry-owned airline sanctioned by the U.S. in May 2023, with Russia's Special Flight Squadron (14 flights) and the Emergency Situations Ministry (12) also active.

C4ADS flagged private carriers that remain unsanctioned despite documented links to Russian military logistics, including Kyrgyzstan-registered Sapsan Airlines. State-owned aircraft typically refueled at Russia's Khmeimim base in Syria and Libyan sites before continuing to the Sahel.
sections.whyItMatters: The flight data underscores how Russia sustains its military footprint in the Sahel through a mix of sanctioned and unsanctioned airlift, and highlights gaps in Western sanctions coverage of the logistics network supporting Russian forces and private military contractors in Africa.

bottomLine: India's Rs 1,577 crore loiter-munition awards to Tata and NIBE — with a Rs 16,000 crore Army drone pipeline and Modi's Independence Day emphasis on indigenous drones — show New Delhi turning battlefield lessons into domestic production. In the U.S., the week's defense industry news was dominated by accountability and competitive dynamics: ProPublica detailed General Dynamics' $533 million artillery plant that produced nothing, the Army picked relative outsider M1 over Bell and Lockheed for a $10 billion training contract, and the Pentagon directed nearly a quarter-billion in no-bid work to Palantir. Separately, Lockheed and Raytheon are hedging on a Ukraine Patriot license amid a drained interceptor inventory, the White House authorized private cyber firms to strike foreign networks, and C4ADS documented a persistent Russian air bridge to the Sahel. The common thread is a defense market reshaped by wartime demand, new entrants and questions about who bears accountability for failed programs.
sources: Defense One, ProPublica, Defense News, Washington Technology, C4ADS, The Atlantic, Financial Times, Breaking Defense, Indian defense news reports (Bing News aggregation)
